newsitem.title: USA: U.S. government warns of poisonous mushrooms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. government warns of poisonous mushrooms.

text.p: Americans should avoid eating wild mushrooms unless they have been identified as non-poisonous by a mushroom expert, federal officials health officials said on Thursday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said three people had died in the United States and 22 were hospitalized in northern California in the past two winters after eating "death cap" mushrooms, which contain toxins not killed by cooking or drying.

A 32-year-old man became ill eight hours after eating mushrooms and died of multiple organ failure nine days later. A 68-year-old man who ate mushrooms he collected on a golf course developed hepatic encephalopathy and died six days later, the CDC said.
It said "death cap" mushrooms are not unique in their appearance and have no distinct taste or smell. The mature mushroom is usually metallic green but can vary from light yellow to greenish-brown.
"This particular mushroom produces a toxin that attacks the liver. Once the toxin gets into the liver cells there's no antidote," CDC epidemiologist Dr. Joel McCullough said.

The species, called Amanita phalloides, accounts for about 90 percent of the deaths from eating mushrooms worldwide. It is primarily found in cool coastal regions of the West Coast but also grows in mid-Atlantic states and in the Northeast.

"Symptoms do not develop for at least six hours after ingestion, so patients may not recognise that their symptoms may be due to mushroom poisoning," McCullough said. "Initial symptoms would be diarrhoea, abdominal pain, signs of dehydration and vomiting."
